name: Neon Red
lede: Neon Red is an extremely saturated red, named for the glow of a neon tube, and a good example of a color no tube of paint and no flat screen swatch can fully reproduce.

sections.title: A glow, not a pigment
sections.body:
Neon Red appears in our library only through the xkcd color survey set, which gives no history for the name [1]. The swatch is very high in chroma, about 92 on the CIELAB scale, and its nearest named neighbor is [[vermilion]] at 6.5 units [1]. Who first used the name as a color is undocumented.

Two of the books use the idea in a useful way. Livingstone lists Neon Red among the Day-Glo paints, whose pigments absorb short-wavelength light and re-emit it at longer wavelengths, so they reflect more light in their band than white paper does [2].

sections.title: Painting a neon sign
sections.body: Gurney describes the problem of painting a red neon bulb on a rainy day [3]. The neon was among the lightest values in the scene and also extremely saturated [3]. White paint was light enough but had no hue, while a light tint of red looked weak, orange or pink, and red straight from the tube was too dark [3]. His compromise was to paint the bulb as a pure red-orange tint and surround it with a wash of midvalue red-orange [3]. A flat screen swatch has the same trouble: it shows the hue, not the light. Compare plain [[red]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive of 23,781 paintings holds one work with a color within six units of this swatch covering at least five per cent of the canvas: Bronzino's [[painting:commons-Q83295755|Pietà with Saint Mary Magdalene]] of about 1529, where it covers 8 per cent [4]. As photographed: museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings; a color match is not a pigment test.

openers: A neon red is a light, not a pigment: paint can only suggest it by value and surround.
Next time you see a red sign at night, notice the pale core and the red halo.
